introduction: Baghdad, the “Abode of Peace,” was Bahá’u’lláh’s home for about eleven years, from the winter journey out of Persia in 1853 to the departure for Constantinople in 1863. These readings are mostly memories, His own and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s: the coffeehouse where strangers were made friends; the road of thirty stages on which not one believer was met; the two years of solitude in the mountains of Kurdistan; the return that revived a dispirited community; a crowded room, a pot of thin soup, an old man smiling at his bread; and the repeated judgment that an exile meant to end the Cause spread it instead. Iraq had received exiles before. The Jews wept by these rivers and were told by Jeremiah to seek the peace of the city; Abraham set out from this country. Their words stand beside the readings, with Paul’s contentment and his “furtherance of the gospel,” Joseph’s “God meant it unto good,” Dante’s salt bread, and Rúmí’s reed cut from its bed. Psalm 137 asks how one can sing in a strange land; these exiles sang all night.
questions: “We would bring the distant near, make the stranger a friend.” Where is your coffeehouse, the ordinary place where you meet those “from within and without”?
The exiles of Psalm 137 hung up their harps; the believers in one small room sang until morning. What accounts for the difference?
Bahá’u’lláh withdrew for two years “lest there should arise … that which would compromise the dignity of the Cause.” When is leaving the right response to conflict, and when is returning?
Thin soup shared by twenty was “the most delicious dinner.” What does your own experience say about comfort and happiness?
“Had this exile not occurred, this joy and glory” would not have come. Joseph and Paul say the same of their misfortunes. Can this be said at the time, or only afterwards?

outside.why: In the coffeehouse of Baghdad, “we would bring the distant near, make the stranger a friend.” Hebrews: be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
Homer’s swineherd gives the oldest reason for it: strangers and foreigners in distress are under Jove’s protection.
Exiles themselves, they sat with “souls both familiar and strange.” Exodus: ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.
The law that follows from that memory: the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself.
In Baghdad Bahá’u’lláh met officials and people Himself. Job’s account of his own house: the stranger did not lodge in the street: but I opened my doors to the traveller.
The grief of exile from Tehran. Dante was told his own banishment in advance: thou shalt abandon everything beloved most tenderly, and learn how savoureth of salt the bread of others.
The first exile of scripture began with a command, and went to the same land in the other direction: get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house.
A long road through towns where there was not one fellow believer. Hebrews on Abraham: he went out, not knowing whither he went.
Thirty stages without a friend, “and now in every one of these stages there are great numbers.” The psalm of the returning exiles: they that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
Frostbite at Asadabad, a sleepless night. Paul’s list of his own travels: in weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness.
The prime minister who banished Him is remembered for it. Jesus at Nazareth: no prophet is accepted in his own country.
A child of nine goes into exile with his Father. Jesus: the foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.

In Iraq He “forbade them to engage in sedition, quarrels, disputes.” Jeremiah wrote to the Jews exiled to the same country: seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives.
Twelve years in Iraq, with the Shah’s permission. Jesus to those he sent out: when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another.
Arriving “in the utmost poverty,” they were “in the supreme station of joy.” Paul: I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.

Exiles had sat beside these same rivers before: by the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a strange land? What made this exile sing?
Bahá’u’lláh withdrew to the wilderness so that dissension might be stilled. Elijah went a day’s journey into the wilderness and sat down under a juniper tree.
Jesus to his disciples: come ye yourselves apart into a desert place.

Two years “in the Kurdish mountains, living solitary and alone in a cave.” Hebrews on the prophets: they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth; of whom the world was not worthy.
Muhammad in the cave on the way to Medina, to his one companion: grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us.
He returned to a dispirited community, and “the Most Great Name flung open the doors.” Hosea: I will bring her into the wilderness, and give her the valley of Achor for a door of hope.
Isaiah on what a return from the wilderness can do for a people: the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.
The Hidden Words were revealed “in a room overlooking the Tigris.” Rúmí’s great poem also begins in exile: hearken to the reed-flute, how it complains, lamenting its banishment from its home.
One who recited the verses “at eventide and at dawn.” The psalmist: in the night his song shall be with me.
The Daystar set in its native land and dawned over Iraq. The Qur’án, to a Prophet soon to emigrate: verily the latter portion will be better for thee than the former.
Many believers in one small room, “and they were very happy.” Sa‘dí: ten dervishes may sleep under the same blanket.
They returned from work and sang all night, and neighbours “who had every comfort” envied them. Ecclesiastes: the sleep of a labouring man is sweet, whether he eat little or much.
One pound of meat for twenty, in a pot filled with water. Proverbs: better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.
Iago, of all people, says the true thing: poor and content is rich and rich enough.
A poor old man looks at each piece of bread, smiles, and thanks God. Paul on a sinking ship: he took bread, and gave thanks to God in presence of them all.
Paul states the old man’s whole economy in a sentence: having food and raiment let us be therewith content.
A visitor asks how large a stipend the chancellor allots. Elijah by the brook had no patron either: the ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning.

“We were strangers and penniless, yet our joy was” great. Emma Lazarus gave a nation’s welcome to such arrivals: give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free. What did Baghdad receive from its exiles, and what did it give them?
In Baghdad “at every moment a new arrow was darted.” Paul: we are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; persecuted, but not forsaken.
“Had this exile not occurred, this joy and glory” would not be. Joseph to the brothers who sold him: ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good.
Persecution intended to end the Cause. Acts: they were all scattered abroad; therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
“If he had not come to Baghdad his cause would not have made such progress in Persia.” Paul from prison: the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel.
Eleven years made the Cause known beyond its country. The Qur’án on emigration: was not Allah’s earth spacious that ye could have migrated therein?

“All were in despair, and yet what great wisdom it contained.” Dante read over a gate the words: all hope abandon, ye who enter in. Who, at the gate of this exile, could have known otherwise, and how?
The departure came “by reason of what the hands of the malicious had wrought.” Moses too left under threat: he fled from the face of Pharaoh, and dwelt in the land of Midian.

Each banishment carried the Faith farther. An early Christian on his own people: every foreign land is to them as their native country, and every land of their birth as a land of strangers. Is exile, for a religion, a misfortune or a condition of its life?
The pilgrim asks the empty House, “Whither is the Ancient Beauty gone?” Lamentations: how doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!
When the returned exiles laid a new foundation, the old men wept and the young shouted, so that the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping.
